title: Restrict first, threaten later
outcomes: Prefers a quiet move that denies the freeing break over a showy pawn push when the opponent is cramped
Checks whether a freeing lever exists before relying on a space edge
Recognises positions where pawn space is not a factor

steps.text: In *Space: count the safe squares, then look for the lever* you counted space. Now choose moves. A *rule of thumb*: when the opponent is cramped, first cover the square of his freeing break with pieces, and only then think about threats. A showy pawn push can hand him the freedom you were denying. Restriction is not passivity: it is a plan.

A space edge helps most when the other side's pieces really lack squares and no pawn lever frees them. If a lever exists, the edge does not bind. In an open position with no pawn space at all, space is not the question; piece activity is. Space also does not grow without limit: breaks and exchanges can undo it.

steps.title: Is the break covered?
steps.prompt: Board 1: White's knight on c3 helps cover d5. Is ...d5 sound for Black? Board 2: one change, the knight stands on d2, so only two pawns attack d5. Is ...d5 sound now? Board 3: do either side's pawns control any square in the other half? Predict each, then check.
In each silent position, which break could the other side use, and did your move cover it, ignore it, or push a pawn instead? Which showy move did you reject?
